This vignette compares Time-Weighted Dynamic Time Warping (TWDTW) [@Maus:2016; @Maus:2019] with random forest
and with a support vector machine (SVM), using the example data that come with `dtwSat`.
It gives an idea of the accuracy and of the processing time of each method. The data set is small,
so the results are an illustration and not an assessment of the methods.

## Data

We read the training samples and the satellite image time series as in the [first vignette](landuse-mapping.html).
There are 291 samples of five land-use classes, and the data-cube has 999 pixels, 23 images, and six bands.

```{r}
library(dtwSat)

samples <- st_read(system.file("mato_grosso_brazil/samples.gpkg", package = "dtwSat"), quiet = TRUE)

tif_files <- dir(system.file("mato_grosso_brazil", package = "dtwSat"), pattern = "\\.tif$", full.names = TRUE)
tif_names <- basename(tif_files)
acquisition_date <- as.Date(regmatches(tif_names, regexpr("[0-9]{8}", tif_names)), format = "%Y%m%d")

dc <- read_stars(tif_files,
                 along = list(time = acquisition_date),
                 RasterIO = list(bands = 1:6))
dc <- st_set_dimensions(dc, 3, c("EVI", "NDVI", "RED", "BLUE", "NIR", "MIR"))
dc <- split(dc, c("band"))
```

To give all methods the same input, we take the time series out of the data-cube as two three-dimensional arrays,
one for the samples and one for all pixels. The first dimension of an array has the time series, the second
the 23 dates, and the third the six bands. For example, `sample_ts[1, , ]` is the time series of the first sample,
with one row for each date and one column for each band.
`twdtw_knn()` and `predict()` work with these arrays in the same way as with the data-cube.

```{r}
bands <- names(dc)
labels <- samples$label

sample_cube <- st_extract(dc, samples)
sample_ts <- sapply(bands, function(band) matrix(sample_cube[[band]], ncol = length(acquisition_date)), simplify = "array")
pixel_ts <- sapply(bands, function(band) matrix(dc[[band]], ncol = length(acquisition_date)), simplify = "array")

dim(sample_ts)
dim(pixel_ts)
```

## Models

We compare four models:

- **TWDTW, GAM patterns**: one temporal pattern for each land-use class, created with a
Generalized Additive Model (GAM), as in the [first vignette](landuse-mapping.html).
- **TWDTW, all samples**: the time series of all training samples are kept as temporal patterns.
- **Random forest**: the package [randomForest](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=randomForest),
with the values of all bands on all dates as predictors.
- **SVM**: the package [e1071](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=e1071), with the same predictors.

TWDTW has the arguments of the [first vignette](landuse-mapping.html), and the other two packages have their default settings.
Each model has a function that trains it with the samples `id`, and `classify()` returns the labels
that a model gives to an array of time series.

```{r}
train_twdtw <- function(id, resampling_fun = NULL) {
  twdtw_knn(x = sample_ts[id, , ],
            y = labels[id],
            time = acquisition_date,
            resampling_fun = resampling_fun,
            cycle_length = 'year',
            time_scale = 'day',
            time_weight = c(steepness = 0.1, midpoint = 50))
}

# One row for each time series, with the values of all bands on all dates
predictors <- function(ts) matrix(ts, nrow = dim(ts)[1])

train <- list(
  "TWDTW, GAM patterns" = function(id) train_twdtw(id, function(data) mgcv::gam(y ~ s(x), data = data)),
  "TWDTW, all samples"  = function(id) train_twdtw(id),
  "Random forest"       = function(id) randomForest::randomForest(predictors(sample_ts[id, , ]), factor(labels[id])),
  "SVM"                 = function(id) e1071::svm(predictors(sample_ts[id, , ]), factor(labels[id])))

classify <- function(model, ts) {
  if (inherits(model, "twdtw_knn")) {
    predict(model, newdata = ts, time = acquisition_date)$prediction
  } else {
    predict(model, predictors(ts))
  }
}
```

## Accuracy

We assess the accuracy with a 5-fold cross-validation: the samples are divided into five groups, and each group
is used once to test a model that was trained with the other four groups. The samples are pixels of a few fields,
and a pixel is similar to its neighbours. With random groups, most test samples would be next to a training sample
of the same field, and the accuracy would be too optimistic. We therefore divide the samples of each land-use class
into five groups of neighbouring samples, using k-means clustering of their coordinates.

```{r}
set.seed(1)

group <- integer(nrow(samples))
for (label in unique(labels)) {
  id <- which(labels == label)
  group[id] <- kmeans(st_coordinates(samples)[id, ], centers = 5, nstart = 20)$cluster
}

accuracy <- sapply(train, function(train_model) {
  sapply(1:5, function(k) {
    model <- train_model(which(group != k))
    test <- which(group == k)
    mean(classify(model, sample_ts[test, , ]) == labels[test])
  })
})
```

The table has the share of test samples with the correct label in percent: the mean of the five groups,
and the lowest and the highest value of a single group.

```{r}
accuracy_table <- data.frame(Mean = colMeans(accuracy),
                             Lowest = apply(accuracy, 2, min),
                             Highest = apply(accuracy, 2, max))

knitr::kable(100 * accuracy_table, digits = 1)
```

All four models classify about 95% of the test samples correctly. The differences between the models are small
compared with the differences between the groups.

## Processing time

To measure the processing time, we train each model with all samples and classify the time series of the pixels.
The data-cube has only 999 pixels, so we classify them ten times to get times that can be compared.
Nine pixels have a missing value in one image. TWDTW classifies such pixels with their remaining observations,
as shown in the [first vignette](landuse-mapping.html), but random forest and SVM need a value for each predictor.
We therefore leave these nine pixels out.

```{r}
complete <- which(complete.cases(predictors(pixel_ts)))
many_ts <- pixel_ts[rep(complete, times = 10), , ]

processing_time <- t(sapply(train, function(train_model) {
  training <- system.time(model <- train_model(seq_along(labels)))[["elapsed"]]
  prediction <- system.time(classify(model, many_ts))[["elapsed"]]
  c(Training = training, Prediction = prediction, Total = training + prediction)
}))

knitr::kable(processing_time, digits = 2)
```

The table has the time in seconds. The two TWDTW models use their time in different ways:

- With GAM patterns, most of the time is training, because a GAM is fitted for each land-use class and band.
The prediction compares each time series with only five patterns, and takes about as long as the prediction of
random forest and SVM.
- With all samples, there is almost no training, but the prediction compares each time series with 291 patterns
and takes much longer.

## Limitations

- The data set is small and covers one year of a small area. The five groups are parts of the same fields,
so the accuracy for another region would be lower for all models.
- The models are used without tuning of their settings.
- The processing time was measured once, on the computer that built this vignette.
- The example has no case in which the time weight of TWDTW is expected to matter,
such as crops with a similar shape of the time series in different seasons.
